subtopics.title: From Raw Data to a Frequency Table

questions.question: Using intervals that include the lower boundary and exclude the upper, a travel time of exactly 20 minutes belongs to:
After tallying, the frequencies 3, 8, 11, 5, 3 must be added because:
options: The sum gives the estimated mean
The sum gives the modal class
Examiners award a mark for addition
The total must equal the number of data values — here 30 — or a value was dropped or double-counted

questions.question: Continuous data such as travel times is grouped into class intervals that should be:
options: Equal in width and covering every value exactly once
As narrow as possible, even if unequal
Chosen so each class has the same frequency

questions.question: In a histogram, the bars touch because:
options: It saves space on the page
The data is continuous — the measurement scale has no gaps between neighbouring classes
The bars are all the same height

questions.question: The bar for the 10-to-below-20 class of the travel data spans 10 to 20 on the horizontal axis and rises to a height of:
A bar graph, unlike a histogram, has gaps between its bars because it displays:
options: Separate categories, with nothing existing between them

subtopics.title: Reading the Shape — Mode, Middle and Skew

questions.question: The modal class of the travel-time histogram (frequencies 3, 8, 11, 5, 3) is:
options: $20$ to below $30$ minutes — the class under the tallest bar

questions.question: With cumulative counts 3, 11, 22, 27, 30, the 15th and 16th values — and hence the median class — lie in:
The estimated mean of the travel times, using midpoints 5, 15, 25, 35, 45, is:
A distribution is called skewed to the RIGHT when:
options: Its peak is on the right
The right side is taller than the left
Its longer tail stretches to the right, with the peak on the left

questions.question: A full analysis comment covers the three slots:
options: Centre, spread and shape — each anchored in context

questions.question: Which sentence would earn the MOST interpretation credit?
options: 'Most learners have short-to-moderate commutes, while a small group travels much longer.'

questions.question: A limitation of any grouped display like this histogram is that it:
options: Cannot show more than five classes
Hides the exact individual values — detail is traded for overview

questions.question: In the bucket picture, each bucket keeps its bottom number and refuses its top one so that:
options: The buckets stay equal in width
Boundary values are counted twice for safety
Every slip has exactly one home — no value lands in two buckets or none

questions.question: The habit of 'counting the counts' after sorting means:
options: Adding the bucket totals and checking they equal the number of slips that went in

questions.question: A raw, unsorted pile of thirty numbers is hard to use because:
options: It reveals no pattern until it is organised

questions.question: In the skyline reading, 'downtown' — the tallest tower — corresponds to the:
'Tall means many, wide means nothing' warns against reading:
options: A bar's width as if it counted people — only height shows frequency
The tallest bar as the mode

questions.question: Favourite school subjects should be displayed as separated towers — a bar graph — because:
options: Bar graphs are easier to draw
The categories are separate; nothing exists between soccer and netball on the axis

questions.question: The three questions of the commenting recipe are:
options: Where is the crowd? How scattered? Is the skyline lopsided?
What is the title? The scale? The colour?
Is it a sample? A census? A survey?

questions.question: The skew of a distribution is named after:
options: The position of the tallest bar
The direction of the longer tail

questions.question: When comparing two histograms, sentences must pair:
options: One graph's mean with the other's range
The tallest bar with the widest bar
Crowd with crowd, scatter with scatter, tail with tail — like with like
